newsitem.title: USA: Ralph Lauren IPO should command designer price tag.
newsitem.headline: Ralph Lauren IPO should command designer price tag.

text.p: Polo Ralph Lauren Corp's sought-after brand name and strong history should guarantee its initial public offering a fancy price tag when it comes to market next week.
"The demand for the deal is extremely high," said Linda Killian, analyst at IPO research firm Renaissance Capital Corp. "It's one of a kind."
The issue comes on the heels of offerings by other fashion houses like Gucci Group NV and Donna Karan International Inc.
The designers have not always dazzled, but others are signing up to join the clique, including Valentino and Gianni Versace.
Polo Ralph Lauren is selling 29.5 million Class A shares in a global offering, with 23.5 million shares slated for the United States. The price range is $22 to $25 a share.
"It's fairly aggressively priced," said Robert Natale, director of equity research at Standard & Poor's, but added that he doesn't expect that to deter investors.
"I think they've done an excellent job of creating a multi-billion dollar company while not diminishing the value of their brand," he said.

Ralph Lauren's successful brand strategy owes much to strict supervision over licensing deals, analysts said. "They've exercised a lot of control over their licensees; they have ultimate approval of everything," said Killian.
Wall Street has had a mixed relationship with the gurus of glamour who have gone public.

Gucci Group, with a share price that has more than tripled from an IPO price of $22, and Donna Karan, with a stock that has fallen about 50 percent from the time of its IPO, provide startling contrasts.

But analysts said that Ralph Lauren should go more the way of Gucci than Donna Karan, citing a well-diversified product base; a clothing line that adopts a more classic, and thereby enduring, look; and greater attention to the bottom line.
As Natale elaborated: "There are no license fees here that go to the founder. The license fees are retained by the company.

"With Donna Karan, (she) and her husband earn money based on revenues. They have never placed the Donna Karan name inside the corporation -- it's still controlled by Donna Karan the person." He said that because the license fees that go to Donna Karan are based on top-line growth, the bottom line could tend to be neglected.

At Ralph Lauren, said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities, "the business has grown, (but) it's not been a rapidly growing business in terms of just haphazardly adding new product lines. You can see that they've added lines with a great deal of study and market knowledge."
Revenues at Ralph Lauren have gone from $846.6 million in fiscal 1995 to $1.18 billion in fiscal 1997, and earnings have increased from $80.2 million to $117.3 million.
Lauren established the Polo brand in 1967 with a collection of men's ties. Today, his company brings together products in apparel, home, accessories and fragrances.

Analysts see good growth opportunities for the firm in many areas, including overseas expansion, further licensing deals, and development of existing businesses like the women's and children's clothing lines and the home products line.
"Ralph Lauren has a great deal of growing to do," said Farley, "It's a got a number of products that are not mature but very entrenched."

According to its filing, the company plans to open five or more additional Polo stores, including flagship stores in London and Chicago, over the next two years. It also intends to add 10 to 20 new outlet stores over three years.
After the issue, the Lauren family will own all the Class B shares -- each entitling the holder to 10 votes -- and thus retain about 89.8 percent of the voting rights.
Affiliates of the lead underwriter, Goldman Sachs, also own 28 percent of the company and are selling stockholders. They could reap about $50 million from the deal.
Ralph Lauren and his family stand to gain about $397 million of the proceeds, based on a share price of $23.50.
